newsitem.title: USA: Dole goes on attack in last debate with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Dole goes on attack in last debate with Clinton.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole ripped into President Bill Clinton's ethical fitness for office on Wednesday night, turning their final campaign debate into a go-for-broke effort to sow doubts about Clinton's leadership.

"Many American people have lost their faith in government. They see scandals almost on a daily basis. They see ethical problems in the White House today," Dole said after a young women asked what he would do to rekindle trust in government.

Dole, far behind in the polls with just three weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election, said "trust is being violated" by the Clinton administration and cited the improper collection of FBI files on top Republicans by Clinton aides an example.
"Young people are looking to us. They're looking to us for leadership. They're watching what we do what we say what we promise and what we finally deliver," Dole said.
"When I'm president of the United States, I will keep my word. My word is my bond," he said.

Clinton seemed unfazed by Dole's attack, ignoring the specifics in his rebuttal but saying in reply to the original question he had "done everything I could at every moment of division in this country ... to bring people together."

The Democratic president took a return shot at Dole with a reference to the highly unpopular move by the Republican Congress to shut down the federal government during a 1995 budget fight. He said the two parties should be working together "instead of shutting down the government in a partisan fight over the budget."
Clinton later accused the Republicans of proposing cuts in the Medicare public health insurance program. That prompted Dole to reply, "There you go again, talking about a Medicare cut."
Dole denied the charge, using the opening to recycle a famous presidential debate one-liner -- "there you go again" used with success by Ronald Reagan in his 1980 debate with Jimmy Carter.
The debate at the University of San Diego followed a town hall format with a heavily white group of 113 undecided voters chosen at random to ask the questions.
Former Republican President Gerald Ford was among those in the audience at Shiley Theater, along with Dole's wife Elisabeth and daughter Robin and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Clinton entered the debate knowing he merely had to avoid mistakes -- as he did in the first debate, on Oct. 6, when most viewers called him the winner -- to hold his commanding position for the last 20 days until the Nov. 5 election.

Only once in recent history has a debate changed the dynamics of a U.S. presidential race. That was in 1980 when Republican challenger Ronald Reagan surged ahead of incumbent Democratic President JImmy Carter on the basis of a strong debate performance in the final days of the campaign.

Dole carried on his attack as the debate proceeded, using a question about whether his age of 73 kept him from understanding the needs of younger Americans to attack Clinton's handling of the war on drugs.
The question brought a stinging reponse from Clinton. "I don't think Senator Dole is too old to be president -- it's the age of his ideas that I question," he said.

It remained to be seen how big a national audience the debate would draw. The TV audience for the first Clinton-Dole debate in Hartford, Conn. on Oct. 6 was estimated at about 46 million viewers, 34 percent fewer than watched the comparable 1992 debate.

Wednesday's debate was competing against a professional baseball playoff game televised on one of the TV networks, leading Dole to report on the score -- Atlanta Braves 1, St. Louis Cardinals 0 -- in his opening statement."
